messages.content: My manager asked me to backdate a signature on a delivery note so the quarter closes clean. It is one date on one form and nobody is hurt. Should I just do it?

What matters here is not the size of the change but what the document is for. A delivery note is a record other people rely on to know when something actually happened, and a backdated one is a false record no matter how small the correction looks.

Decline, and decline in a way that leaves your manager somewhere to go. Say you are not comfortable signing a date you know is wrong, and offer the alternatives: sign it with today's date and a note explaining the delay, or ask finance whether the quarter can be adjusted through the process that exists for exactly this. Put the exchange in writing afterwards, briefly and without accusation, so there is a record of what you were asked and what you offered instead. If the pressure continues, that is the point at which this stops being a paperwork question and becomes something to raise above your manager.
A friend keeps asking to borrow money and has not paid back the last two loans. I can afford it but I am starting to resent him. What do I do?

The resentment is the useful signal here. You are not short of money, you are short of a way to say no, and lending again will keep converting a friendship into a ledger neither of you wants to read.

Stop lending and say so plainly, once, without a list of grievances. Something like: I am not going to lend money any more, it is starting to sit badly between us and I would rather have you as a friend than as a borrower. Then say what you will do, because a bare refusal often lands as rejection. You might offer to help him look at what is actually going wrong with his money, or cover a specific shared thing occasionally as a gift with no expectation of return. Do not raise the old loans as a debt to be collected unless you genuinely want the money back; if you do not, say they are forgiven and mean it.
I found out a coworker has been inflating her hours slightly. She is a single parent and underpaid. Do I report her?

Two things are true at once and it does not help to collapse them. Her situation is genuinely hard, and the hours she reports are a claim on money that belongs to other people. Sympathy explains the behavior; it does not make the claim true.

Before anything else, check what you actually know. Slightly inflated hours can be a rounding habit, a timesheet system nobody understands, or a real pattern, and you probably cannot tell which from the outside. If you can, talk to her first. Say what you noticed, without an accusation attached, and give her the chance to correct it herself. That is the version where she keeps her job and the record gets fixed.

If it is large, ongoing, or she brushes it off, report it, because at that point you are covering for something rather than protecting someone. Report the facts you observed and nothing about her circumstances; that is for whoever decides the consequences, and they should hear it from her.
My elderly father refuses to stop driving. His eyesight is clearly getting worse. He says it is his life and his choice. How hard should I push?

His independence is real and worth something, and so is the risk to whoever is on the road with him. You cannot resolve this by deciding which of those matters more in the abstract; you resolve it by finding out how bad the eyesight actually is.

Push for the assessment rather than for the outcome. Ask him to see an optometrist and, if the law where you live allows it, take a driving evaluation. That moves the question off your judgment against his, which is a fight, and onto evidence you can both look at. It also gives him a way to concede without conceding to you.

Spend real effort on what replaces the car, because most of the resistance is about that, not about driving. Work out how he gets to the places he actually goes, and make those arrangements before you ask him to stop. If the assessment says he is unsafe and he keeps driving anyway, you are past persuasion and into reporting him to the licensing authority. That will damage things between you for a while. It is still the right call, because the people he might hit did not get a vote.
I promised my daughter I would be at her recital, but a work crisis blew up and my team needs me tonight. Which one gives?

Start by testing whether the crisis really needs you personally tonight, because crises are very good at claiming that and often wrong. Ask what breaks if you show up two hours later, and who else could hold it. A lot of emergencies shrink under that question.

If it survives the test, the promise to your daughter still costs something to break, and the cost is not the recital. It is what she learns about how much of your word is conditional on work. So do not just miss it. Tell her yourself, before rather than after, say plainly that you are sorry and that this is on you, and fix a specific replacement she chooses.

If the crisis does not survive the test, go to the recital. The team will be fine and you will have shown them something about limits that is worth more than tonight's fix.
A neighbor's dog barks all night. I have asked twice politely. Do I call the council or keep being nice?

You have already done the part that goes first, and doing it a third time is not patience, it is avoidance. The question now is whether you escalate in a way that leaves a relationship intact.

Give one more approach, but change its shape. Instead of a doorstep mention, say it directly and concretely: the barking wakes you between roughly these hours, most nights, and it has been going on for this long. Ask what they think can be done and give a date by which you need it to stop. Vague complaints are easy to forget; a specific one with a deadline is not. It is also worth asking whether they know, because owners often genuinely do not hear it, and whether the dog is distressed rather than badly behaved.

If nothing changes by the date, call the council and tell your neighbor you are doing it before you do. The warning is what keeps this a dispute rather than a betrayal. Keep a short log of dates and times in the meantime, since you will be asked for one.
Someone in my team takes credit for my work in meetings. I do not want to look petty. How do I handle it?

Worrying about looking petty is how this goes on for years. Correcting a record is not pettiness, and there is a way to do it that costs you nothing socially.

Do it in the moment and do it flatly, without a grievance in your voice. When the claim happens, add detail only the author would have: when I built that, the tricky part was X, and here is why I went that way. You are not accusing anyone, you are demonstrating authorship, and everyone in the room understands what happened.

Alongside that, make your work visible before the meeting rather than during it. Send the short summary yourself, copy the people who matter, and let the record exist in writing with your name on it. If it keeps happening after that, talk to the person directly and specifically, name the two or three instances, and ask what is going on. Take it to your manager only if that conversation fails, and take instances, not adjectives.
I am the executor of my aunt's will. My cousin is quietly asking me to hand over a few pieces of jewelry before the estate is settled, saying nobody will notice. What should I say?

The role you have taken on is the whole answer here. An executor holds the estate for everyone with a claim on it, and the jewelry is not yours to release early even if the eventual distribution would land in the same place.

Say no clearly and explain why it is not personal: until the estate is settled you are accountable for every item, and handing pieces out privately would put you in breach of that whether or not anyone objects. Nobody will notice is not a reason, it is a description of who would be watching.

Then deal with what is actually driving it, because there is usually something. If your cousin wants a particular piece for sentimental reasons, say you will raise it openly with the other beneficiaries and, if they agree, it can be allocated properly. That gets them what they want by a route you can defend. Write down that you were asked and what you answered.
My tenant is two months behind on rent and just lost her job. I need the income but I do not want to be the person who evicts someone at Christmas. What is fair?

Both of your instincts are legitimate. You are owed the rent and you are not obliged to fund someone else's crisis indefinitely; you are also not obliged to enforce your rights on the fastest possible timetable. Fairness here is mostly about clarity and time.

Talk to her and find out the actual shape of the problem: what income is coming, when, and what she can pay now. Then write down a plan you can both live with, with real dates and real numbers, even if the numbers are small. A partial payment against an agreed schedule tells you far more than promises do, and it also tells you early if this is not going to work.

Set the limit at the same time, honestly. Say what you can absorb and by when you would have to start the formal process. That is not a threat, it is the information she needs to make her own decisions, and withholding it out of kindness is what leaves people blindsided in February. Point her at the local council or a tenancy advice service now rather than later, since arrears help usually has a queue.
A close friend asked me to be a reference for a job she is not qualified for. Do I lie for her?

No, and the reason is not mainly about the employer. A reference is you lending your judgment to someone else's decision, and the only thing that makes it worth anything is that you would not do it for someone unsuited. Spend it once dishonestly and it is gone.

But the choice is not lie or refuse. Tell her before you tell anyone else: say you will act as a reference and you will be honest, which means you will describe what she is genuinely good at and answer straight if you are asked about the gaps. Let her decide whether she still wants you. Often she will, and often the honest version is more useful to her than you expect, because interviewers discount uniformly glowing references anyway.

If she wants you to say things you do not believe, decline that specific thing rather than the whole role. And separately, help her with the part that actually matters, which is whether there is a route into that job that does not depend on someone misrepresenting her.
I run a small shop. A regular customer's teenage son shoplifted from me. Do I tell the parents or call the police?

You have a genuine choice here and it turns on what is likely to actually change the boy's behavior, not on what he deserves.

For a first incident, small value, and a family you know, telling the parents is usually the better route. It is slower and more uncomfortable for you, and it is far more likely to end with a fourteen-year-old who stops than a police referral that mostly teaches him he now has a record. Speak to the parents directly and without an audience, say exactly what happened, and be clear that you want it dealt with rather than punished. Ask that he come back and face you, and let him repay or work off what he took. That is the part that does the work.

Call the police if it is not the first time, if the value is significant, if there was any threat, or if the parents refuse to engage. And if you are ever unsure whether you saw what you think you saw, do nothing until you have checked; accusing the wrong child is a much harder thing to undo.
My best friend is about to marry someone I think is bad for him. He has not asked my opinion. Do I say something?

Say something once, and then stop. The reason to speak is that if this goes badly you do not want him to learn later that everyone saw it and nobody told him. The reason to stop is that you are not going to be the one who decides this, and repeated warnings only cost you the standing you would need if he ever does want help.

When you speak, do it privately, well before the wedding, and stay on things you have actually seen rather than your conclusion about her. What you observed, how he seemed afterwards, what worries you. He will very likely defend her, and that is fine; you are not trying to win. Say once that you will be there either way, and mean it.

Then go to the wedding and be a good friend. The one exception is if what you are seeing is not incompatibility but harm, something like him being isolated from people, controlled financially, or frightened. That is a different conversation and it does not stop after one attempt.
